top_choice_rationale: P001 (B020, Helpman and Melitz) is the contribution that most changed what economists measure and how they evaluate policy. Melitz (2003) moved trade analysis from the industry to the firm and produced sharp selection and reallocation predictions that firm-level data in many countries have tested for over two decades. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) added the exporting-versus-FDI margin, and the framework has spread into industrial organisation and quantitative macro. The work is mature, and the two names fit the originating model and its first major extension. The main weakness is the credit boundary with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not on the credited list. I judge this manageable through a mechanism-centred citation and a Scientific Background that sets out the empirical precursors. The welfare magnitudes also depend on parametric assumptions, so the qualitative mechanism is better supported than the quantitative gains. P002 (B001) is a close second. It has cleaner attribution and equal maturity, but weaker and more mixed empirical confirmation. P004 (B019) is third because its design-based evidence is credible, although the persistence debate and the task-theory attribution questions remain. P003 (B016) is fourth because constitutional identification is weaker and its marginal case is reduced by the 2024 institutions prize. No award is last because each proposal is a substantial, mature contribution. I do not count the 2008 trade prize or the number of first-place supporters as merit.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile. It lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Helpman, Melitz, Grossman, Persson, Tabellini, Besley, Autor, Hanson or Dorn. My field is corporate finance and financial contracting, which is not close to trade. Disclosed ties are to committee colleagues (long overlap with Hassler, Krusell, Ellingsen and Svensson) and to the Academy as KVA Vice President, not to any candidate. Not adjudicated.
